summary: Defines, with a companion document, an inter-autonomous system routing protocol for the Internet. This is version 3 of BGP. It was on the standards track and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: BGP-3 lets independently administered networks tell one another which destinations they can reach and which autonomous systems a route crosses. This version uses an initial full table followed by updates when reachability changes, and the RFC is now marked Historic.

questions: what are the bgp message types
subtitle: BGP version 3 exchanges network reachability and path information between autonomous systems.

tldr.problem: Autonomous systems need to exchange which networks they can reach and the path traffic would take, while allowing routing loops to be detected and some policies to be applied.
tldr.mechanism: BGP-3 uses TCP port 179, sends a full routing table when a session starts, and then sends incremental UPDATE messages with routes and path attributes.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1267 is Historic and obsoletes RFC 1163. It describes BGP version 3; its companion RFC 1268 describes how BGP is applied in the Internet.

today: RFC 1267 is marked Historic and obsoletes RFC 1163. Its companion, RFC 1268, describes how BGP is applied in the Internet; RFC 1267 itself says security issues are not discussed.

sections.title: What BGP-3 Exchanges
sections.content:
The Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is an inter-autonomous-system routing protocol. A BGP speaker shares network reachability information with other speakers, including the sequence of autonomous systems traffic must cross to reach a network.

Each autonomous system advertises to its neighbors only routes it uses itself. This hop-by-hop approach lets BGP construct a graph of autonomous-system connections, detect routing loops, and support some policies. The RFC says policies that require source routing are outside this model.
sections.plainLanguage: BGP speakers exchange reachable networks and the autonomous systems on each route. This path information helps detect loops and apply policies that work with hop-by-hop routing.

sections.title: Starting a Session and Sending Updates
sections.content:
Two speakers establish a transport connection and exchange messages to open and confirm the session. They send the entire routing table first, then send incremental updates as routes change. They do not periodically resend the complete table, so each speaker keeps its peers' current tables for the life of the connection.

BGP uses TCP on port 179. Speakers exchange KEEPALIVE messages to show the connection is active. If an error occurs, a NOTIFICATION is sent and the connection closes. Connections between speakers in different autonomous systems are external; connections within one autonomous system are internal.
sections.plainLanguage: At the start of a session, the speakers exchange their routing tables. After that, they send only changes and use KEEPALIVE messages to show the connection is still active.

sections.title: The BGP Message Header
sections.content:
Every BGP message begins with a fixed 19-octet header. It contains a 16-octet Marker, a 2-octet Length, and a 1-octet Type. The Length counts the entire message and must be at least 19 and no greater than 4096 octets.

The four message types are OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION, and KEEPALIVE. OPEN carries the sender's autonomous-system number, BGP version, hold time, identifier, and authentication fields. UPDATE carries path attributes and network numbers. NOTIFICATION reports an error and is followed by connection closure; KEEPALIVE contains only the header.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message starts with a 19-octet header that gives its length and type. The type tells the peer whether the message opens a session, changes routes, reports an error, or confirms that the connection is active.

sections.title: Attributes That Describe a Route
sections.content:
Each UPDATE includes path attributes that describe the routes it carries. The RFC defines ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, UNREACHABLE, and INTER-AS METRIC. For example, AS_PATH lists the autonomous systems traffic would cross, and NEXT_HOP identifies the border router to use next.

All implementations must recognize well-known attributes. Optional attributes may be unfamiliar to some speakers: an unknown optional transitive attribute is retained and passed on with its Partial bit set, while an unknown optional non-transitive attribute is ignored. A route whose AS_PATH already contains the local autonomous system cannot be selected as a better route because doing so would create a loop.
sections.plainLanguage: Route attributes say where a route came from, which networks it crosses, and which router is next. A speaker rejects a route that already contains its own autonomous system in the path.

sections.title: The Six Session States
sections.content:
The BGP finite state machine has six states: Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, and Established. It begins in Idle, starts a transport connection, sends OPEN, confirms the peer with KEEPALIVE, and reaches Established before exchanging UPDATE messages.

Connection failures, invalid messages, hold-time expiration, or other specified errors can send the session back to Idle. When an Established session closes, the speaker removes the routes it learned through that connection. If both peers start a connection at the same time, they use their BGP identifiers to decide which connection to keep.
sections.plainLanguage: A BGP session moves through connection, opening, confirmation, and established states. If the connection or message exchange fails, the speakers close the session and remove routes learned through it.

sections.title: Errors, Route Withdrawal and Policy Limits
sections.content:
When a speaker detects an error in a message, it sends a NOTIFICATION with an error code and optional diagnostic data, then closes the connection. An UPDATE can mark a previously reachable route as unreachable. Before switching from a route that has become unreachable, the speaker must advertise that loss to the neighbors that previously received the route.

Routing policies are not exchanged by BGP. The RFC notes that policies across several autonomous systems can conflict and cause route oscillation. BGP-3 includes a rule that can help speakers notice some contradictions, but does not provide a mechanism to stop the resulting oscillation. The RFC's Security Considerations section says security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A speaker reports a failed route before replacing it, so neighbors can distinguish a broken route from one that is merely less preferred. BGP-3 does not solve oscillation caused by conflicting policies, and its security issues are not discussed.

fields.name: Marker
fields.desc: 16 octets; used for synchronization and, when defined, authentication.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total message length, from 19 to 4096 octets.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Identifies OPEN, UPDATE, NOTIFICATION, or KEEPALIVE.
